title: The lost book (2 Kings 22)
hook: workmen find the law in the temple, and young King Josiah tears his clothes
carry: the book was lost in the house

segments.voice: Yesterday, a frightened servant at Dothan, and a prayer: open his eyes. Your line was more with us. What help did you find when you counted again? Day seven hundred thirty-eight.

A renovation is under way. Carpenters, builders and masons are working on the temple in Jerusalem, and the money for timber and hewn stone is being counted out. The king is Josiah. The text says he became king at eight years old, and this is the eighteenth year of his reign. Somewhere in the work, the high priest Hilkiah comes across something and sends word to the king's scribe, Shaphan, in one plain sentence: "I have found the book of the law in the house of the LORD." Found. In the house of the Lord. Where, you'd think, it should never have gone missing. Today is what happens when the king hears it read.
screen: `I HAVE FOUND THE BOOK OF THE LAW.`

segments.voice: Shaphan reads it to himself, then carries it to the king and reads it aloud. And the text says: "when the king had heard the words of the book of the law, that he rent his clothes." Josiah hears words that were in his own temple the whole time, and he tears his clothes. The text never says how the book went missing. No theft, no fire. Some readers picture it lost the quiet way things get lost in a busy house: under other things, while everyone was occupied with the building. Then Josiah does something interesting. He doesn't ask the priests to explain it to him. He sends them to enquire of the Lord, and they go to a prophet, a woman, Huldah, who lives in Jerusalem. Her answer is hard news for the city, but for the king there's a tender line. In the King James Bible, the word to him is: "Because thine heart was tender, and thou hast humbled thyself before the LORD." What saves the moment is not that Josiah already knew. It's that, hearing it late, he let it reach him. And in the next chapter he gathers everyone, small and great, and reads the whole book to them himself. Which book was it? The chapter calls it the book of the law and doesn't say more. Some readers connect it with Deuteronomy. Whatever it was, the story puts the loss somewhere uncomfortable: not out in the world, but inside the house of worship, among people working hard on the building.

Here's the practice: find one book you've lost in the house. Settle, and breathe. Let your mind walk through your rooms, real or not. Is there a book you've let gather dust: a Bible, a letter, a journal, something that once meant a lot? Or a word someone said to you that you've stopped rereading? Don't scold yourself. Josiah wasn't the one who lost it, and he still let it reach him. Just find it, and picture picking it up. If you pray, you can hold it before God for a moment. If you don't, just hold it, and let it be found. The bell holds the time.
The lost book. The book of the law, found in the temple during repairs, read aloud to a young king who tore his clothes.
Your line: the book was lost in the house. Today, reread one thing you've neglected, even a single page, and let it reach you. Day seven hundred thirty-eight.

howItsDone: Some Christians mark a return to Bible reading by remembering Josiah's discovery, and churches sometimes use 2 Kings 22 to encourage people to read scripture for themselves and aloud together.

fork.reveal: Josiah rends his clothes and sends his men to enquire of the LORD, and they go to Huldah. the word to him: because thine heart was tender.

original.note: Hebrew: the book of the law, what Hilkiah says he found in 2 Kings 22:8.

trapdoor: what you thought: a lost book is a library problem.
what it means: the book went missing inside the temple itself, and a young king tore his clothes when he finally heard it.
what a scholar hears: Huldah, a woman prophet in Jerusalem, is the one the king's men go to, and the next chapter has Josiah read the book to everyone, small and great.

notes: Josiah's age (eight) and 'the eighteenth year' are from 2 Kings 22:1 and 22:3.
'Tearing your clothes is what people in these stories do at a death' is a general observation (e.g. 2 Samuel 1:11, 3:31); confirm phrasing.
Spoken quotation of 22:19 is to the king via Huldah; the KJV verse is 'Because thine heart was tender, and thou hast humbled thyself before the LORD, when thou heardest...'. Partial quote.
The Deuteronomy identification is attributed to 'some readers' only; confirm the Keeper is happy to mention it.
Original: סֵפֶר הַתּוֹרָה; confirm pointing and pronunciation.
